Is there a cross-platform (Win, Mac, Linux) library in Node.js / Python / C++ that just returns all the GPU stats like shading cores, clock, available instruction sets (or FP32, FP64 FLOPS values) so I could calculate the max theoretical performance myself? $\begingroup$ As a partial answer I believe what you are calling "threads" is a trick that allows for a core to host what looks like two threads at a time (hyper-threading) while only real having one actual physical core to compute with. * Similarly, with SIMD instructions, a core can do the same operation on multiple pieces of data at the same time -- say, add four pairs of floating point numbers together, yielding 4 FLOPs at the same time. * $\begingroup$ You might also discuss how SIMD floating-point units can increase the theoretical peak performance. I wish there was at least a formula that would approximate the actual FLOPS performance just from the time it takes for CPU to compute a specific function. Now I should mention that the latest GPUs also have dedicated matrix calculation units and even though their theoretical peak far outperforms the FMA theoretical peak, they are typically measured separately since they have a bit of a niche use case and their performance alone doesn't translate well to anything that isn't mostly pipelined matrix operations which is most things, even games. 1. A 1.3 GHz 768 core GPU will have the max FMA performance of 1.3(GHz) x 768(cores) x 2(because FMA is technically two calculations in one instruction) = 1996.8GFLOPS. 2. A 2.8 GHz 4 core CPU with AVX256 will have the max FMA performance of 2.8 x 4 x 2 x 8(because you can do 8 32b instructions with a 256b SIMD instruction) = 179.2GFLOPS. This means that GPU shaders have to be polished to extreme levels to reach anywhere near half of the theoretical peak whereas with CPU's you just need to make sure that you are using SIMD instructions where appropriate (something that modern compilers are pretty good at doing automatically). 0") CPU and GPU influence on task parallel execution performance.

results.title: How fast is a single GPU core compared to a CPU core? - Quora
results.content: How fast is a single GPU core compared to a CPU core? > 1 GPU SIMD unit (with only 32 threads) is 6 times slower than 1 CPU core. > 1 GPU core 4 times faster than 1 CPU core. GPU and CPU cores can’t really be compared to each other like this, as they are designed for different types of processes. GPU and CPU cores can’t really be compared to each other like this, as they are designed for different types of processes. Comparing a single GPU core to a single CPU core is not a one-number question; they are different designs optimized for different workloads. Comparing a single GPU core to a single CPU core is not a one-number question; they are different designs optimized for different workloads. * Practical result: for highly parallel, vectorizable compute (dense matrix multiply, stencil, convolution), one GPU core participates in delivering far higher aggregate FLOPS per dollar and per watt; per‑ALU instantaneous FLOPS are lower than a full CPU core’s simulated peak, but GPUs have massively more ALUs and higher memory bandwidth, so total throughput is much larger. * Memory bandwidth: GPUs provide much higher device memory bandwidth (hundreds of GB/s) than a single CPU core’s effective memory bandwidth (a few GB/s per core), so memory-bound kernels run far faster on GPU. * A single CPU core can often deliver higher performance on small, latency-sensitive tasks. * For highly parallel linear algebra or convolution: a single modern GPU (entire device) can be 10–100× faster than a single high-end CPU core for the same algorithm; per-core comparisons are not directly meaningful but reflect that GPUs trade complex per-thread logic for greater parallel ALU count and memory bandwidth. * For single-threaded, latency-sensitive code: one CPU core is typically faster than one GPU SM (streaming multiprocessor) or the equivalent collection of GPU ALUs because of lower latency, richer control, and better caching. * Branch-heavy small-function work: CPU core often 2–10× faster than launching a GPU kernel and moving data. For parallel, vectorizable, bandwidth-hungry workloads, the GPU’s aggregate performance far exceeds a CPU core; for latency-sensitive, irregular, or serial tasks, a CPU core performs better.

results.content: Do modern GPUs have enough FLOPS, texture Fillrate and Memory Bandwidth to keep up with their own Pixel Fillrate and not get self-bottlenecked? For a 3D game to run at 120fps, a GPU has (let’s just say 2000) GPU cores. A 5GHz CPU can compute the locations of a complex wireframe vertex array very quickly, while a GPU has tools and storage specifically designed to render textures and lighting effects to bring the wireframe to life. Short answer: Modern GPUs are designed with balanced ratios between compute (FLOPS), texture fillrate, pixel (render) fillrate, and memory bandwidth, but no single fixed proportion prevents self-bottlenecking across all workloads. Short answer: Modern GPUs are designed with balanced ratios between compute (FLOPS), texture fillrate, pixel (render) fillrate, and memory bandwidth, but no single fixed proportion prevents self-bottlenecking across all workloads. For gaming GPUs that target high-res rasterization, memory bandwidth and ROP throughput are often scaled up relative to shader FLOPS to avoid being ROP/memory-limited. For example, 100–500 GFLOPS per GB/s is a plausible ballpark for desktop GPUs running typical game shaders with compression/caching; compute-heavy workloads (AI, physics) require much more bandwidth per FLOP. + Desktop GPUs for 4K gaming increase memory bus width/GDDR speed and ROP resources to avoid being fillrate-limited at high resolutions, while also adding compression hardware to amplify effective bandwidth. Is it possible to know if the CPU will bottleneck GPU? The way to force your fps down to that level (again, if the game is capable of it) is to max out every graphical setting you can, thus forcing the fast GPU to do a ton of work and allowing the CPU to catch its breath a bit by running at maybe 86% instead of 99%. results.title: How Neural Networks Leverage GPUs: From FLOPs to Memory and Precision
results.content: # How Neural Networks Leverage GPUs: From FLOPs to Memory and Precision. In this article, we explore how GPUs power neural networks by dissecting the key components: floating point operations per second (FLOPs), memory, precision support, interconnects, and the nature of parallelism itself. GPUs are particularly well-suited for neural network computation because the core operations, such as matrix multiplications, dot products, and convolutions, are mathematically deterministic and inherently parallelizable. High-bandwidth memory (e.g., HBM3e in H100/H200/B200) allows data to be fed to compute units without bottlenecks, enabling GPUs to operate closer to their FLOPs ceiling. ### Conclusion: The Right GPU for the Right Job. In deep learning, FLOPs determine your ceiling, memory defines your scope, precision affects your stability, and interconnects determine your scalability. As we move into the age of trillion-parameter models and real-time AI agents, understanding how neural networks interact with GPU hardware isn't just technical trivia; it's strategic infrastructure knowledge.
